claims.text: Challenge table, five rows: server time and own root (drivers 1, 2; no next step); old statements after a leak (revocation, audit log; none); own HSM (ADR 0023's reason, ADR 0022's reopen condition; none); TSA down at month end (risk, backend developer); second bank (open, team lead).
The review's ranked drivers: (1) checkable for many years, even after the certificate ends; (2) a leaked key's damage limited in time; (3) no key outside an HSM.

The bank trusts only roots it names; the server's time fails driver 2 because whoever holds a leaked key can set the server clock back to before the revocation, so a signer-supplied time proves nothing.
claims.source_hint: docs/design/bank-signing-design-review.md @ stage-4 lines 58-59, 103; docs/adr/0029-*.md @ stage-4 lines 22-24

claims.text: The lab sample InvoiceCertificates.cs trusts a root of Đơn Hàng's own that the bank does not trust and sets RevocationMode.NoCheck, so it does not check revocation.
The bank checks a package alone: signature, chain to a trusted root, timestamp from a trusted TSA giving the signing time, then the saved revocation status showing the certificate valid at that time.

After a revocation, statements timestamped before it stay valid and later ones do not; a pre-revocation statement the audit log does not list never went through Payments' logged signing path, so it is treated as suspect.
claims.source_hint: docs/design/bank-signing-design-review.md @ stage-4 line 104; docs/adr/0015-*.md lines 39-41; docs/design/audit-log.md lines 27-37

claims.text: ADR 0015: the invoice key is in an HSM only Payments may call; whoever takes over Payments can get signatures only while in control and cannot take the key; the HSM signs whatever an allowed caller sends, so Payments limits its requests and logs each in the audit log.
ADR 0029: every request to sign, to timestamp and to fetch status writes an audit log entry.
An own HSM is rejected for ADR 0023's reason, repeated in ADR 0029: devices in two places and people to run them; the bank key lives in the provider's HSM service (ADR 0015, 0023).

ADR 0022 chose a provider's managed Kubernetes, tied to the provider's key service (ADR 0023), and reopens on a contract demanding own machines or data in a set place; a contract demanding the key on own machines meets the condition of 0022 and 0023, and a new ADR replaces 0023 for this key only.
claims.source_hint: docs/adr/0022-*.md @ stage-4 lines 1, 40-41, 52, 76-80; docs/adr/0023-*.md lines 45-49; docs/adr/0029-*.md lines 61-63; review lines 94-95

claims.text: Risk: TSA failing at month end near the bank's deadline; owner backend developer; next step: sign from the first day of the month, retry over many hours, tell the bank if the deadline gets close.
The bank's deadline is the fifth working day of the next month (assumed); a statement may wait a few hours to be signed (assumed).
A second bank needing statements is one of ADR 0029's review conditions; the review leaves 'one key per bank?' open, owner team lead.

claims.text: ADR 0015 rejected a SealedSecret for the invoice key: Payments reads it at start, so the key sits in Payments' memory and whoever takes over Payments can copy it and keep signing after the fix; the gateway's API key is kept that way (ADR 0006).
ADR 0029: if the HSM, TSA or CA fails, the statement waits and is retried within a few hours; taking orders and refunds are not affected.
After a revocation, no past statement needs a new signature; ADR 0029 has no step that signs stored statements again.

claims.text: Answer a challenge from the driver, ADR or risk already written; when a case is not covered (TSA outage, second bank), record a risk or open row with an owner rather than redesigning in the session.
When a second bank wants statements, the team records whether each bank gets its own key in a new ADR rather than adding the bank to the existing key in a quick change.
